491.title: With great joy (Luke 24:50–53)
491.hook: he blesses them as he's carried up, and they return with great joy
491.tomorrow: In the beginning was the Word
491.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Ascension of the Lord forty days after Easter (moved to the following Sunday in many dioceses), and the Mass ends each time with the priest blessing the people before they are sent out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last evening in that room: he opened their understanding. Your line was opened. Today, the last page of Luke.

How do you say goodbye to someone you won't see again in this life? An airport curb, a hospital bed, a last visit with a grandparent. A goodbye like that can empty a person out: the quiet drive home, the minutes sitting in the car before going inside. Luke's Gospel ends with a goodbye too. But the people in it don't go home quiet. They go home, of all things, with joy.
screen: `THE LAST GOODBYE.` → `A QUIET DRIVE HOME.` → `THESE GO HOME WITH JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the ending, in the Douay-Rheims: "And he led them out as far as Bethania: and lifting up his hands, he blessed them." While he is blessing them, he is parted from them and carried up to heaven. His last gesture in this Gospel is a blessing, hands lifted the way a priest blesses, still doing it as he goes. Then: "And they adoring went back into Jerusalem with great joy." They had every reason for grief. Why joy? He gave them understanding. He promised power from on high. And he left blessing them, so the last thing they saw was not his absence but his care. Now look where Luke ends: in the temple, always praising and blessing God. Where did this Gospel begin, about fifty days ago on this path? In the temple, with an old priest named Zachary, struck silent at the altar, unable to speak to the people waiting outside. Some readers see a frame: a priest who couldn't speak to the people at the start, and at the end, hands lifted in blessing and people blessing God in return. Between them, the whole Gospel: the angel and Mary, the manger, the boy in the temple, the sermon at Nazareth, the lost and found, the cross, the road to Emmaus. Joy runs through it, from the angel's good tidings of great joy at Bethlehem to this last line. And Luke wrote a second volume, the Acts of the Apostles, which tells the ascension again, more fully, with forty days and a cloud. Catholics celebrate that day as the Ascension of the Lord.

segments.voice: Picture someone you said goodbye to today, even an ordinary goodbye, a kid at school drop-off, a coworker leaving, a parent on the phone, going on with their evening. Wish them good on purpose: their sleep, their worries, their tomorrow, so the last thing you hold tonight is care, not absence. If you pray, ask God to bless them by name; if you don't, just send them the wish.

Your line: great joy. And that's the Gospel of Luke, fifty days, from Zachary in the temple to great joy in the temple. Tomorrow, John begins.

492.title: In the beginning was the Word (John 1:1–5)
492.hook: the light shines in darkness and the darkness did not comprehend it
492.howItsDone: Catholics hear John's prologue at the Mass of Christmas Day, and again on the Second Sunday after Christmas where that Sunday is kept.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bethania: a last blessing, and disciples who went home with great joy. Your line was great joy. Now, a new Gospel.

Matthew starts with a family tree. Mark starts with a man shouting in the desert. Luke starts with an old priest in the temple. John starts before anything started. No Bethlehem, no shepherds, no Jordan River. Just: in the beginning. Those are the first words of the whole Bible, the opening of Genesis, before light, before land, before anyone. John borrows them on purpose. For the next six weeks we read the fourth Gospel in order, and on day one it reaches back past the first day of creation.
screen: `MATTHEW: A FAMILY TREE.` → `MARK: A VOICE IN THE DESERT.` → `JOHN: BEFORE ANYTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening, in the Douay-Rheims: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." Today's word is John's, logos. In Greek it means a word, but also reason, an account, the meaning behind things. Greek philosophers had used logos for the order running through the universe. Jewish readers knew of God's word that creates, and of Wisdom, who was with God at the making of the world. John takes all of that and says something none of them said: the Word was with God, and the Word was God. Then: "All things were made by him: and without him was made nothing that was made." Not a star, not a cell, is outside him. In him was life, and the life was the light of men. "And the light shineth in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it." Comprehend is a lovely double word: understand, and also grasp, get hold of. The darkness didn't understand the light, and couldn't get hold of it either. Translators have argued for centuries which John meant; many think both. Saint Augustine remembered the old priest Simplicianus telling him that a Platonist philosopher used to say these opening lines deserved to be written in letters of gold and set up in every church. On Christmas Day the Church reads them at Mass, so the baby in the manger is heard with this first: before Bethlehem, the Word.

493.title: The Word was made flesh (John 1:9–14)
493.hook: and dwelt among us; Catholics once genuflected at this line in nearly every Mass
493.howItsDone: Catholics bow at the words of the Incarnation in the Creed and genuflect there on Christmas and the Annunciation; those who pray the Angelus traditionally kneel at "and the Word was made flesh".

segments.voice: Yesterday, logos: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God. Your line was the word was God.

Et Verbum caro factum est. In the old Latin Mass, the Mass is over, or nearly. The priest has given the blessing, and now he walks to the left side of the altar and reads in Latin from the first chapter of John, a reading called the Last Gospel. The people are standing. They know where this is going. They are waiting for one line. When it comes, priest and people go down on one knee together. Then they stand again.
screen: `THE OLD LATIN MASS.` → `THE PRIEST READS JOHN IN LATIN.` → `EVERYONE KNEELS AT ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: Before the line, John tells a hard truth. The true light came into the world, and the world, made by him, didn't know him. "He came unto his own, and his own received him not." But some did, and to them he gave power to become children of God. Then the line: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." In Latin, Et Verbum caro factum est. That's where they knelt. Yesterday the Word was with God before creation. Today the same Word has skin, and hunger, and a mother. Flesh is a blunt word: not a body, or a human nature, but the soft, mortal, breakable stuff we're made of. Then dwelt. The Greek verb literally means pitched his tent, and readers hear in it the tabernacle in the desert, the tent where God's glory came to dwell among Israel. John goes on: "and we saw his glory, the glory as it were of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth." The Church calls this the Incarnation, from the Latin for in the flesh. The genuflection at the Last Gospel is mostly gone now, since that reading left the ordinary form of the Mass after the Second Vatican Council. But the gesture lives on. In the Creed, at the words about the Son becoming man, Catholics bow; on Christmas and the feast of the Annunciation, they kneel at those words instead. Those who pray the Angelus traditionally kneel at this very line. The body bends at the moment God is said to take a body.

If you pray, let the bow be your prayer; if you don't, just notice what it is to bend your body at a thought.

494.title: Come and see (John 1:29–39)
494.hook: John points, two disciples follow, and Jesus asks what seek you
494.howItsDone: At every Mass the Lamb of God (Agnus Dei) is sung or said while the priest breaks the host, and just before Communion he holds it up and repeats John the Baptist's words, behold the Lamb of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, eskenosen: the Word was made flesh, and pitched his tent among us. Your line was and dwelt among us.

Bethania, beyond the Jordan. John is baptizing there when he sees a man walking toward him, and he points. What he says next is a line the priest repeats at Mass just before Communion, lifting the host: behold the Lamb of God. It didn't come from a council or a liturgist. It came from a riverbank. Today, that line, and what two people do the moment they hear it.
screen: `BETHANIA, BEYOND THE JORDAN.` → `A MAN WALKING TOWARD HIM.` → `A LINE NOW SAID AT MASS.`

segments.voice: John the Baptist sees Jesus coming and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world." Lamb of God is a strange thing to call a man. Readers hear in it the Passover lamb, whose blood marked the doors in Egypt, the lambs offered every day in the temple, and Isaiah's servant, led as a sheep to the slaughter. John packs all of that into one name. The next day he says it again, and two of his own disciples hear him, leave him, and follow Jesus. Jesus turns, sees them trailing behind, and speaks his first words in this Gospel: "What seek you?" Not who are you, not what do you believe. What are you looking for? They answer with a question of their own: Rabbi, where do you live? And he says: "Come and see." No sermon, no test, just an invitation to come along and look. They came, saw where he abode, and stayed with him that day; John even remembers the hour, about the tenth hour, late in the afternoon. One of the two was Andrew. The other is never named; some readers have thought it was the writer himself, remembering the afternoon his life turned. The Church keeps John's pointing finger at the center of the Mass. The Lamb of God is sung while the bread is broken, and then the priest lifts the host, points as John pointed, and says: behold.

If you pray, tell God plainly what you're seeking; if you don't, just let yourself hear your own answer.

495.title: Under the fig tree (John 1:43–51)
495.hook: Nathanael asks can anything good come from Nazareth
495.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Bartholomew on August 24, and on that day the Mass reads this Gospel of Nathanael under the fig tree, following the old tradition that they are the same man.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Agnus Dei: John pointed, and two disciples followed and heard, come and see. Your line was what seek you.

Some towns come with a reputation. The one up the highway with nothing but a gas station. The neighborhood a family warns its kids about. Then a friend runs up, breathless: we've found him, the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, and he's from there. That's today's scene. A man named Philip has just been called, and he goes straight to his friend Nathanael with the news. And Nathanael, hearing the name of the hometown, says out loud exactly what he thinks of it.
screen: `A TOWN WITH A REPUTATION.` → `PHILIP: WE'VE FOUND HIM.` → `HE'S FROM NAZARETH.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims, Nathanael answers: "Can any thing of good come from Nazareth?" That's his whole review of the place. Philip doesn't argue. He uses the words Jesus said to the first two disciples the day before: come and see. Nathanael comes, and as he walks up, Jesus says of him: "Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no guile." No guile, no trickery. It's almost a joke: the man who just insulted Jesus's town is praised for being honest. He said exactly what he thought. Startled, Nathanael asks how Jesus knows him. And Jesus says: before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you. We aren't told what happened under the fig tree. Some readers imagine Nathanael was praying or studying there, but nobody knows. What matters is that Nathanael knows, and it undoes him. In one breath the skeptic says: Rabbi, thou art the Son of God, thou art the King of Israel. Jesus answers: you believe because I said I saw you under the fig tree? You will see greater things than these. An old tradition identifies Nathanael with the apostle Bartholomew. If that's right, the man who sneered at Nazareth became one of the twelve. The good thing came from the place he'd written off.

496.title: The first sign (John 2:1–11)
496.hook: John calls miracles signs: they point past themselves
496.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Wedding at Cana as the second of the Luminous Mysteries of the rosary, usually on Thursdays, and often take Mary's words to the servants as a short summary of her role.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fig tree: a skeptic asked if anything good could come from Nazareth, and came to see. Your line was can any good thing come.

A road sign that says Chicago, 40 miles is not Chicago. Nobody pulls over and takes a selfie with it as if they've arrived. Its whole job is to point somewhere else. Today's word is sign, the word John chooses, again and again, for what the Douay-Rheims calls miracles. And the first one happens somewhere you wouldn't expect: not in the temple, not at a sickbed, but at a village wedding in Cana of Galilee, on the third day, when the wine runs out.
screen: `A ROAD SIGN ISN'T THE CITY.` → `JOHN'S WORD FOR MIRACLES.` → `A WEDDING IN CANA.`

segments.voice: Mary is the one who speaks up: "They have no wine." Just that. His answer sounds cool to our ears: woman, what is that to me and to thee? my hour is not yet come. Woman is the same word he will use for her from the cross, and Mary seems to hear something other than no. She tells the servants: "Whatsoever he shall say to you, do ye." They're her last recorded words in John's Gospel. There are six stone water jars, used for the Jewish rites of washing, each holding two or three measures. Fill them with water, he says, and they fill them to the brim. Draw some out, and take it to the steward. The steward tastes it, has no idea where it came from, and calls the bridegroom over: everyone serves the good wine first, and the poorer wine once the guests have drunk well, "But thou hast kept the good wine until now." John closes it this way: "This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee; and manifested his glory, and his disciples believed in him." Where the Douay says miracles, John's Greek says signs, semeia. A sign isn't the destination. It points to who he is. Here, water for washing becomes wine for a feast. Saint John Paul the Second made Cana one of the Luminous Mysteries of the rosary, so those who pray the rosary come back to this wedding, and to Mary's words to the servants.

segments.voice: Go back over today slowly, like flipping through photos on your phone, and look for one small thing that pointed past itself: a kindness out of nowhere, a meal that tasted better than it should, a moment that felt like more than it was. Don't force it into anything big; just notice where it pointed. If you pray, thank God for it; if you don't, let it be a sign of something good.

497.title: Nicodemus by night (John 3:1–8)
497.hook: born again of water and the Spirit; the Church hears baptism here
497.carry: the wind bloweth where it will
497.howItsDone: The Catholic Church reads John 3:5 as speaking of baptism, the new birth by water and the Spirit, and this passage is often read at baptisms and in the Easter season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first sign at Cana: water for washing became wine for a feast. Your line was the good wine until now.

Some questions only come out at night. At two in the morning, a person asks what they couldn't ask at lunch. Today a man comes to Jesus with that kind of question, and John tells us he came by night. His name is Nicodemus: a Pharisee, a respected teacher, a ruler among his people, a serious student of the scriptures. He has seen the signs, and he's honest about it. Rabbi, we know you are a teacher come from God; nobody could do these signs unless God were with him. And Jesus answers a question he hasn't asked yet.
screen: `QUESTIONS THAT COME AT NIGHT.` → `A RESPECTED TEACHER.` → `RABBI, WE KNOW.`

segments.voice: Jesus says: "Amen, amen I say to thee, unless a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." The Greek word translated again, anothen, can also mean from above. Born again, born from above; John seems to want both. Nicodemus takes it literally and asks the almost comic question: can a grown man go back into his mother's womb? Jesus goes further: "unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God." This is where the Catholic Church hears baptism. The Catechism calls baptism a new birth by water and the Spirit and points to this very verse. Since the earliest centuries, Christians coming up out of the font have been called newly born. Then a picture. In Greek, pneuma means both wind and spirit. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, reads it as Spirit: "The Spirit breatheth where he will; and thou hearest his voice, but thou knowest not whence he cometh, and whither he goeth." Many other English Bibles, the King James among them, read it as wind, blowing wherever it will, and today's line holds that reading. Both are faithful to the Greek. You can't see the wind or steer it; you hear it in the trees and see what it moves. Nicodemus, the careful scholar, is told this new birth is not something he can schedule. And John will bring him back twice, the last time carrying a hundred pounds of spices to the tomb.
screen: `BORN AGAIN, BORN FROM ABOVE.` · `WATER AND THE HOLY GHOST.` · `PNEUMA: WIND AND SPIRIT.` · `NICODEMUS WILL BE BACK.`

segments.voice: Let a question come that you usually keep for the dark, about God, yourself, someone you love, what happens after, and don't answer it; just let it be asked, the way Nicodemus asked his. You're allowed to ask it. If you pray, bring it to God as it is; if you don't, just hold it honestly.
Anothen. The Greek word meaning both again and from above, at the heart of Jesus' answer to Nicodemus in the dark. Today's word.
Your line: the wind bloweth where it will. And that's week seventy-one: great joy, logos, the Word made flesh, Agnus Dei, the fig tree, the first sign, and Nicodemus.
screen: `WEEK SEVENTY-ONE: JOY · LOGOS · FLESH · AGNUS DEI · FIG TREE · SIGN · NICODEMUS`
